# Introduction


Many studies now use a surrogate outcome, such as a machine-coded or AI-generated score, when the outcome of interest is expensive to obtain.
The surrogate may be available for every unit, but it is not the actual outcome.
If the surrogate is systematically off, estimates based on it alone can also be off.

Mozer and Miratrix [-@mozer2025more] describe one way to use a human-coded subsample to correct this bias.
The researcher codes a random subset of units, compares the human-coded outcomes to the surrogate outcomes in that subset, and uses the observed differences to adjust the full-sample surrogate estimate.
Mozer, Pashley, and Miratrix [-@mozer2026stratified] extend this idea by asking which units should be selected for human coding.
When surrogate errors vary across observable groups, stratified sampling can reduce uncertainty by making the human-coded sample more informative.
This package, `stratsampling`, provides the code to implement the methods in these works.

In this vignette, we provide an overview of the package, walking through the workflow of selecting a sample for coding and then estimating final treatment impacts with both the machine predicted and the human coded data.
We also show how to conduct power calculations to assess the possible costs and benefits of human coding a stratified subsample of the full dataset.


## Installation

To use this package, first load it after installing it from GitHub (you may need to install `devtools` from CRAN to make the following code run, and you only need to run the install line once as it will install it permanently on your computer):

```{r setup, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("lmiratrix/stratsampling")
library(stratsampling)
```


# A complete workflow

The example uses the package's built-in toy dataset.
Pretend these data come from an RCT where you have a machine-coded outcome that is a proxy for some outcome that would be expensive to obtain.
The workflow has five steps: load data, choose a stratification, draw a sample, merge the coded outcomes, and estimate the treatment effect.


## Step 1: Load the data

Suppose you have data from an RCT with a machine-coded surrogate
outcome (`Yhat`) for every unit.
The true outcome is expensive to obtain, so it will only be observed for a human-coded subsample.
The dataset also contains baseline covariates and a treatment indicator:

```{r}
data( toy_data )
head( toy_data )
```


The `toy_data` dataset contains `r nrow(toy_data)` observations with
three baseline covariates (`X1`, `X2`, `X3`), a surrogate prediction
(`Yhat`), treatment assignment (`Tx`), and a unique identifier (`ID`).
`X3` is known to be highly predictive of the actual outcome.


## Step 2: Create and evaluate candidate stratifications

The first design choice is how to stratify the population.
The `create_stratification_candidates()` function generates candidate stratifications based on different variables and numbers of strata:

```{r}
candidates <- create_stratification_candidates( toy_data,
                                                vars = c("Yhat", "X1", "X2", "X3"),
                                                Z = "Tx" )
length( candidates )
```

Each candidate is a factor vector assigning every observation to a stratum.
To compare candidates before coding, use `compare_stratifications_precoding()`.
This ranks the candidates using proxy metrics based only on the surrogate outcome and observed covariates:

```{r}
comparison_precoding <- compare_stratifications_precoding( toy_data,
                                                           candidates,
                                                           Z = "Tx" )
head( comparison_precoding )
```

The results are sorted by promise, with the best choice at top.
We might select `Yhat_quintiles` as our choice, but given subject matter expertise we might also choose a different one that we believe is worth focusing on.
For example, in this case, we know that `X3` is a strong predictor of how well we are able to predict the outcome, so we might include it.
We could directly use `Yhat_X3_3x3` as our choice, or we could use the `make_interaction_strata()` function to make a custom stratification that is based on the interaction of `Yhat` and `X3`.

Here we decide to make a 3 x 3 stratification of `Yhat` and `X3`:

```{r}
toy_data$strata <- make_interaction_strata( x1 = toy_data$Yhat, 
                                            n1 = 3, 
                                            var_name1 = "Yhat",
                                            x2 = toy_data$X3, 
                                            n2 = 3, 
                                            var_name2 = "X3",
                                            z_vec = toy_data$Tx)

# The above is equivalent to pulling from the candidate library:
alt_strat <- candidates[[ 'Yhat_X3_3x3' ]]
all.equal( toy_data$strata, alt_strat )
```


## Step 3: Draw a stratified sample

With the stratification fixed, draw the human-coded sample using
`generate_sample_index()`.
By default, the function samples proportionally within strata:

```{r}
toy_data$sample <- generate_sample_index( toy_data, 100,
                                          Z = "Tx", strata = "strata",
                                          seed = 4044 )
table( toy_data$strata, toy_data$sample )
```

Note our 9 strata with around 10% of the documents being coded in each.
The code will attempt to sample proportional to strata size, unless told otherwise.

The table shows that each of the 9 strata contributes roughly 10% of its documents to the coded sample.

To create a coding sheet for human coders:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sheet <- toy_data %>%
  filter( sample == 1 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( ID ) %>%
  mutate( Yobs = NA ) %>%
  arrange( ID )
write_csv( sheet, "coding_sheet.csv" )
```


## Step 4: Merge coded outcomes

After coding, merge the human-coded outcomes back into the full dataset:

```{r}
data( "toy_data_coded" )
toy_data_coded

full_data <- toy_data %>%
    left_join( toy_data_coded, by = "ID" )

# Verify all targeted documents were coded
table( sampled=full_data$sample, has_outcome = !is.na( full_data$Yobs ) )
```

The next table summarizes surrogate bias and residual error within each stratum:

```{r}
sum_stat <- full_data %>%
  group_by( strata ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_code = sum(sample),
             mean_Yhat = mean( Yhat ),
             mean_Y = mean( Yobs, na.rm=TRUE ),
             bias = mean_Yhat - mean_Y,
             err = sd( Yobs - Yhat, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  arrange( -mean_Yhat )
sum_stat
```

Because the stratification crosses `Yhat` and `X3`, we can plot bias and residual error across `Yhat` levels within each `X3` group:

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
sum_stat_plot <- sum_stat %>%
  separate( strata, into = c("Yhat_strat", "X3_strat"), sep = " / " ) %>%
  mutate( Yhat_strat = factor( Yhat_strat,
                               levels = c( "Low Yhat", "Med Yhat", "High Yhat" ) ) ) %>%
  pivot_longer( cols = c(bias, err),
                names_to = "stat", values_to = "val" )

ggplot( sum_stat_plot, aes( Yhat_strat, val,
                            col = X3_strat, group = X3_strat ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ stat, scales = "free_y" ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 0, linetype = 2 ) +
  labs( x = "Yhat stratum", y = "Value", color = "X3 stratum" ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

When bias differs across strata, the stratified estimator corrects those differences within strata rather than averaging them over the full sample.
The residual error panel (`err`) shows whether some strata have noisier surrogate predictions than others.
If that heterogeneity is large, optimal allocation may be worth considering.


## Step 5: Estimate the treatment effect

The `est_ma_strat()` function computes the stratified model-assisted estimator.
It combines the full-sample surrogate predictions with within-stratum bias corrections estimated from the coded subsample:

```{r}
es <- est_ma_strat( data = full_data,
                    Yobs = "Yobs",
                    Z = "Tx",
                    S = "sample",
                    strata = "strata",
                    Yhat = "Yhat" )
es
```

The main outputs are `est` (the ATE estimate) and `SEhat` (the estimated standard error).
For comparison, we can also compute the SRS model-assisted estimator, which ignores the stratification:

```{r}
es_srs <- est_ma_srs( data = full_data,
                       Yobs = "Yobs",
                       Z = "Tx",
                       S = "sample",
                       Yhat = "Yhat" )
es_srs
```

Because the sample was stratified, this SRS calculation is not the estimator we would use for inference.
It is included only to show how the standard errors compare in this example.


# Power analysis

Before collecting human-coded outcomes, it is useful to ask how much coding is needed to reach a target level of precision and how much stratification changes that calculation.

First estimate the design parameters from pilot data:

```{r}
R2s <- estimate_R2( full_data, Yobs = "Yobs", Yhat = "Yhat",
                    Z = "Tx", strata = "strata" )
R2s
```

Then plot MDES (minimum detectable effect size) curves as a function of the coding fraction:

```{r, messages=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
target_MDES <- 0.25
pp <- plot_power_curve( nrow(full_data), mean(full_data$Tx), 1,
                        R2_ML = R2s$R2_ML, R2_strat = R2s$R2_strat )

# Plot with target MDES line
pp +
  geom_hline( yintercept = target_MDES, lty = 3 ) +
  scale_y_continuous( breaks = seq(0, 0.3, by = 0.05) ) +
  expand_limits( y = 0 )
```

The underlying values are stored as an attribute of the plot:
```{r}
tbl <- attr( pp, "table" )
head( tbl )
```

Use the table to find where each curve is closest to the target MDES:
```{r}
crosses <- tbl %>%
  group_by( Method ) %>%
  filter( abs(MDES - target_MDES) == min(abs(MDES - target_MDES)) )
crosses
```

In this toy example, the stratified design reaches the target at about an 11% coding fraction.

The ratio of required sample sizes tells us how much stratification
reduces the coding burden:

```{r}
1 - crosses$h[[1]] / crosses$h[[2]]
```

Here, stratification reduces the required coding effort by about 27%.
